Hellinger enrichment for subject-level compositions

GW McElfresh

Methods: Paul Edlefsen

2026-10-20

Source: vignettes/hellinger-enrichment.Rmd
hellinger-enrichment.Rmd

Understanding whether categorical compositions differ between experimental groups is critical when you summarize single-cell annotations to subject-level frequencies. The unit of inference is the donor (or animal, or replicate), whose multinomial counts define a composition vector on a probability simplex. Cell-level cluster proportions can look sharply different while subject-level compositions remain exchangeable across groups, and the reverse can hold when sampling noise is large relative to an imposed enrichment. Real cohorts rarely reduce to a single pairwise comparison, so this vignette uses three groups: a Control, a Condition1 group with an imposed enrichment, and a Condition2 group that remains exchangeable with Control. Here, we illustrate HellingerDistanceEnrichment on that synthetic cohort, separating the conceptual framework (distance, ratio, contrasts, inference) from the worked analysis that recovers which comparisons differ.

Concepts

Paul Edlefsen developed the inferential core below: Hellinger geometry on Jeffreys-softened subject compositions, the between/within distance ratio RR, observed-inclusive label permutation, and collapse/subset contrasts. The Dirichlet Bayes option instead draws subject compositions from a conjugate posterior, so composition uncertainty carries into every statistic the package reports.

Composition enrichment

Composition enrichment asks whether experimental groups occupy different regions of the simplex once you aggregate cells to subjects. At the cell scale, each row carries a category label (cluster, cell type, module score bin) and metadata that links that cell to a subject and a group. At the subject scale, those labels become counts: for subject ss and category kk, we observe cskc_{sk} cells (or events) in category kk, and the subject’s composition is the normalized frequency vector ps=(cs1,…,csK)/∑kcskp_s = (c_{s1}, \ldots, c_{sK}) / \sum_k c_{sk}.

The scientific question is relational. We ask whether between-group compositional distance exceeds within-group compositional distance across subjects, and leave aside which category dominates any one subject. That framing mirrors pseudobulking in expression analysis: many cells collapse to one replicate-level observation, and hypothesis tests must respect the replicate as the unit of inference. A cluster enriched at the cell level within a single subject does not, by itself, establish group-level enrichment, because one subject’s multinomial draw can dominate the apparent pattern.

This package tests enrichment by comparing the average pairwise Hellinger distance between subjects in different groups to the average pairwise distance between subjects in the same group. The output is an effect-size ratio plus a p-value from label permutation on fixed compositions, or, under the Bayesian option, the posterior probability that the ratio exceeds 1 (PPGT1) from Dirichlet composition draws. Either way, the package breaks the result down into an omnibus summary and contrast-specific results.

Hellinger distance

Once you normalize counts to frequencies, compositions live on a simplex, and Euclidean distance on raw proportions is a poor geometry: scaling one category compresses the others, and small zeros carry disproportionate weight. Hellinger distance measures separation between two frequency vectors pp and qq by comparing their square roots:

H(p,q)=12∥p−q∥2∈[0,1]. H(p,q)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left\lVert\sqrt{p}-\sqrt{q}\right\rVert_2 \in [0,1].

Values near 0 indicate similar compositions; values near 1 indicate near-disjoint support. The package computes HH from count vectors by forming frequencies internally, so it measures distance on normalized compositions, never on raw counts.

Sparse categories create a second problem: empirical frequencies of zero are not credible endpoints when counts are small. Before computing distances, the package softens counts with a Jeffreys-style pseudocount. For subject ss, category kk, and default α=1/2\alpha = 1/2,

c̃sk=csk+α,psk=c̃sk∑jc̃sj. \tilde{c}_{sk} = c_{sk} + \alpha, \qquad p_{sk} = \frac{\tilde{c}_{sk}}{\sum_j \tilde{c}_{sj}}.

The default priorPseudocounts = 1/2 matches the conjugate Dirichlet prior used in the Bayesian approach. Softening pulls extreme proportions toward the simplex center and stabilizes pairwise distances when some categories are rarely observed.

Hellinger distance answers whether compositions are separable in frequency space. It does not, by itself, identify which category drives a contrast, establish causality, or correct for differences in total cell yield between subjects beyond what the normalized frequencies encode. Biological interpretation still requires knowing what the categories represent and whether the aggregation level matches the experimental question.

The enrichment ratio

Given a subjects-by-categories count matrix, the package builds a symmetric subject-level Hellinger distance matrix DD, where Dss′=H(ps,ps′)D_{ss'} = H(p_s, p_{s'}) using softened, normalized compositions. It then groups subjects by experimental label gg and, for each group pair (g,g′)(g, g'), summarizes distances as mean pairwise Hellinger distance within or between subject sets:

  • Within-group (diagonal of the group summary): mean of Dss′D_{ss'} for subjects s,s′s, s' both in group gg.
  • Between-group (off-diagonal): mean of Dss′D_{ss'} for subjects ss in group gg, s′s' in group g′g'.

The enrichment effect size is the ratio of average between-group distance to average within-group distance:

R=H¯betweenH¯within. R=\frac{\overline{H}_{\mathrm{between}}}{\overline{H}_{\mathrm{within}}}.

When R>1R > 1, subjects in different groups are farther apart, on average, than subjects within the same group under this metric. When R≈1R \approx 1, group labels are consistent with exchangeable compositions relative to the observed within-group dispersion. The ratio rests on pairwise subject distances, so each group must contribute at least two subjects; otherwise within-group means are not identifiable and inference stops with an error.

This ratio is the test statistic for both permutation and Bayes methods. It compresses a full distance matrix into a single scale-free quantity that you can compare across contrasts and posterior draws.

Contrasts

A contrast is a specified comparison among group labels on which the package evaluates RR. The package always computes an omnibus contrast that includes all group levels present in the composition object. Without contrasts, it also computes all pairwise contrasts ((G2)\binom{G}{2} comparisons). If you pass contrasts, those specifications become the contrast family: the package skips auto pairwises, so you pay the permutation Holm adjustment only on the comparisons you named. Set includePairwise = TRUE if you still want the full pairwise set in addition to your specs.

The analogy to differential expression is deliberate but not exact. In DE, a contrast selects linear combinations of model coefficients on log-expression. Here, a contrast selects which subjects enter the between/within distance summaries: all groups (omnibus), a pair of groups (subset), or a remapped grouping (collapse). A length-2 character vector is one pairwise comparison. A list may mix those vectors with collapse or subset lists; names become contrastId values, and unnamed elements get A_vs_B identifiers.

Two levels of reporting matter in practice:

  • Permutation: result$omnibus$pValue is the unadjusted p-value for the global between/within ratio; result$contrasts$pValue and pAdj are contrast-specific, with pAdj applying Holm adjustment across the contrast table by default (pAdjustMethod = "holm").
  • Bayes: result$omnibus$PPGT1 and result$contrasts$PPGT1 are the posterior probability that R>1R > 1; R_PPGTnope and E_PPGTnope are the posterior probabilities that RR and EE clear their NOPE edges (R_nopeHigh, E_nopeHigh); R_hdiAboveNope and E_hdiAboveNope are TRUE when the 95% HPDI sits entirely above that reported edge. There is no pAdj; pAdjustMethod is unused.

Omnibus and pairwise contrasts answer nested questions. A significant omnibus result indicates that at least some group separation exists under the ratio metric; pairwise contrasts localize that separation, with multiplicity control on the contrast table rather than on the omnibus line.

Permutation and Bayes answer different questions

Both methods use the same between/within ratio RR; they differ in whether they hold composition vectors fixed.

Permutation (method = "permutation"). The package estimates compositions once from softened counts, which fixes the subject distance matrix. It then permutes group labels among subjects BB times (nPermutations) and recomputes RR on each shuffle. The one-sided p-value includes the observed statistic in the numerator:

p=#{Rperm≥Robs}+1B+1. p=\frac{\#\{R_{\mathrm{perm}}\ge R_{\mathrm{obs}}\}+1}{B+1}.

This tests whether group labels are exchangeable given the estimated compositions. It does not propagate uncertainty in the multinomial allocation of cells to categories.

Bayes (method = "bayes"). For each posterior draw, the package samples subject compositions from a conjugate Dirichlet posterior. With Jeffreys increment α\alpha,

ps∼Dirichlet(cs⋅+α), p_s \sim \mathrm{Dirichlet}(c_{s\cdot} + \alpha),

where cs⋅c_{s\cdot} is the count vector for subject ss. The package rebuilds the full Hellinger distance matrix from that draw and recomputes RR and EE. Across nPosterior draws, it reports:

  • posterior-mean RR (effectSize),
  • posterior probability that R>1R > 1 (PPGT1),
  • posterior probabilities that RR and EE clear their NOPE intervals, permutation-calibrated null reference intervals set by label shuffling (R_PPGTnope, E_PPGTnope), with the median upper bound of each interval (R_nopeHigh, E_nopeHigh) and whether the 95% HPDI sits entirely above that edge (R_hdiAboveNope, E_hdiAboveNope), described below,
  • 95% highest posterior density interval on RR (effectCiLow, effectCiHigh), the shortest window containing 95% of the draws.

PPGT1 is P(R>1)P(R > 1). R=1R = 1 is the exchangeability reference for the metric (between-group distances match within-group distances on average), not a threshold for a practically large enrichment. You read closeness to 1 from the interval and from the posterior draws, including result$omnibus$draws and the omnibus rows of result$draws. Equal-tailed central posterior intervals remain available via credibleInterval = "cpi". HPDI is the better default when the posterior of RR is asymmetric near 1, because a quantile interval spends equal mass in both tails even if one tail is a long, empty stretch.

By sampling compositions instead of fixing them, the Bayesian approach propagates multinomial uncertainty into RR. When counts are sparse, that can widen credible intervals or lower PPGT1 relative to a permutation p-value on the point estimate, even when point ratios look similar. When counts are dense, Dirichlet draws concentrate around the same frequencies used by permutation, so a ratio that sits only slightly above 1 can still have PPGT1 near 1: composition-sampling noise is small relative to a 1-2% bump in RR, while label permutation still finds that bump easy to produce by chance. The two methods then disagree without either being misspecified, because they answer formally different questions. With dense counts and a strong imposed enrichment, as in the synthetic example below, they often agree on which contrasts rise above 1.

NOPE: a permutation-calibrated null reference for the Bayes output

Dense counts are the usual case for single-cell data, where each subject contributes hundreds or thousands of cells, and that is where PPGT1 misleads. The Dirichlet posterior only describes count noise within each subject, so it treats the sampled subjects as the whole population. If groups do not differ, the sample RR still lands a little above or below 1, and as depth grows the posterior shrinks onto that chance value. In the sampling-depth vignette’s simulation (10 categories, 8 versus 8 subjects drawn from identical populations, 100 cohorts per depth), 27% of cohorts reported PPGT1 > 0.95 at 2000 cells per subject and 25% at 500, against 1% at 50 cells per subject. A threshold of exactly 1 therefore means something different at different depths.

The defaults nope = "shuffle" and energyNope = "shuffle" set a Null-Oriented Permutation Equivalence (NOPE) interval on each statistic: a permutation-calibrated null reference interval for conditional effects. The interval is conditional in two senses: on the observed design (group sizes, depths, within-group spread) and on each posterior draw’s compositions. The goal parallels a permutation test, but NOPE reports a region instead of a p-value. Within each posterior draw, the package shuffles group labels nNopeShuffles times (default 200) on that draw’s distance matrix and takes the 95th percentile of the shuffled RR and of the shuffled EE as the upper edges of their NOPEs. Shuffling keeps the group sizes, depths, number of categories, and within-group spread, so each edge is the largest value these subjects routinely produce when labels carry no information; in that simulation the RR edge sat near 1.06 at every depth, and R_PPGTnope > 0.95 fired in at most 1% of the null cohorts.

R_PPGTnope is the posterior probability that RR clears its edge, and E_PPGTnope the same for EE; R_nopeHigh and E_nopeHigh are the median edges across draws. We floor each draw’s edge at the no-difference value (1 for RR, 0 for EE), so R_PPGTnope can never exceed PPGT1. The 95% HPDI (effectCiLow to effectCiHigh) is the credible interval on the statistic; the NOPE is the permutation null region. R_hdiAboveNope is TRUE when that HPDI sits entirely above the reported NOPE (effectCiLow > R_nopeHigh); E_hdiAboveNope is the same comparison for EE. We recommend reading the NOPE probabilities as the headline Bayes result and keeping PPGT1 as the exchangeability reference. Take heed of the threshold, though: a cutoff of 0.95 asks nearly every draw to clear its own shuffle edge, so it runs well below a 5% false-positive rate and loses power, most of all at shallow depth (R_PPGTnope > 0.95 detected 1% of 5-point shifts at 50 cells per subject, against 50% for the permutation test). In the same simulation R_PPGTnope > 0.5 tracked the permutation test at 500 and 2000 cells, and the sampling-depth vignette reports the same comparison for E_PPGTnope and for R_hdiAboveNope. Setting nope or energyNope to "none" drops that statistic’s columns. A fixed seed gives different posterior draws with and without a NOPE, because its shuffles consume random numbers between Dirichlet draws; fixed edges consume none.

Very small groups cannot support a NOPE, for the same reason they cannot produce a small permutation p-value. With 3 versus 3 subjects there are only 10 distinct ways to split them, so the true split alone is 10% of all shuffles and neither statistic can clear its 95th percentile. If the true split is at least 5% of shuffles, the package warns, reports both NOPE probabilities as NA instead of a misleading 0, and sets enoughShufflesForNope to FALSE so the reason stays attached to the result; 4 versus 4 is the smallest balanced design that supports it.

NOPE and Kruschke’s ROPE

NOPE borrows the equivalence logic of Kruschke’s region of practical equivalence, or ROPE (Kruschke, 2018, Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science 1:270-280) and departs from his procedure in two ways. In Kruschke’s ROPE, the analyst fixes the region before seeing the data, from domain knowledge of which effects are negligible, and the decision compares the 95% highest density interval with that region. That works when the parameter has familiar units, such as a difference in means. Few of us have that intuition for a ratio of mean Hellinger distances or for an energy distance, so the NOPE takes its edge from the data: the largest value of the statistic these subjects routinely produce when group labels carry no information. The edge also differs from draw to draw, and each NOPE probability counts the draws that clear their own edge. The NOPE therefore behaves as a null threshold set from label shuffles, closer to a permutation test than to a statement of practical significance.

If you know the smallest effect that matters, pass it as a fixed NOPE bound, which plays the role of Kruschke’s preset region: a number above 1 for nope on RR, or a number above 0 for energyNope on EE. For EE, ComputeEnergyNopeBound() turns a composition shift into a bound: give it the reference and shifted compositions, and it returns 2(1−BC)2(1 - \mathrm{BC}) with Bhattacharyya coefficient BC=∑kpkqk\mathrm{BC} = \sum_k \sqrt{p_k q_k}. The bound is exact when every subject sits at its group’s mean and approximate otherwise. Fixed edges need no shuffles and work for groups too small for the NOPE; when neither statistic keeps a NOPE, the run draws no extra random numbers. The worked example below shows the default NOPEs and fixed edges side by side.

Energy distance alongside the ratio

Both methods also report the energy distance between groups. We build it from the same subject distance matrix as RR, but square each Hellinger distance first:

E=2H2¯12−H2¯11−H2¯22. E = 2\,\overline{H^2}_{12} - \overline{H^2}_{11} - \overline{H^2}_{22}.

We average EE over group pairs for the omnibus (energyDistance; Bayes adds energyCiLow and energyCiHigh). Squaring makes EE the squared distance between the two group centroids in square-root composition space, less the sampling spread each centroid carries. RR measures how far apart the groups are relative to how spread out they are, while EE measures the shift in mean composition itself, with no division. If every subject sits at its group centroid, E=2(1−BC)E = 2(1 - \mathrm{BC}) between the centroids, which is why the fixed energyNope above can start from a composition shift. The sample estimate leaves out each subject’s distance to itself, so it can dip slightly below 0 when groups do not differ.

For a single two-group contrast with similar spread and depth in both groups, the two statistics usually lead to the same call. They part ways in a few common situations:

  • Unequal heterogeneity. If one condition (e.g. disease) is more variable than control, its spread dilutes RR even when the shift is real; EE reports the shift directly.
  • Ranking contrasts. When pairwise contrasts differ in within-group spread, ordering them by RR mixes effect with noise; EE orders them by the shift alone.
  • Very homogeneous groups. When subjects within each group are nearly identical, a tiny shift can produce a large RR; EE shows that the shift is small in absolute terms.
  • Different depths or studies. Count noise at low depth adds to between- and within-group distances alike, which pulls RR toward 1. With squared distances that noise cancels from EE in expectation, although Jeffreys softening still shrinks both statistics at shallow depth. In the sampling-depth simulation, EE keeps about half its noise-free value at 25 to 50 cells per subject, while the excess of RR over 1 keeps about a third, so EE compares more fairly across cohorts, batches, and studies.

The trade runs the other way when groups differ in spread but not in mean composition: RR and its tests respond strongly, while EE moves only slightly. The p-values and PPGT1 stay on RR; under Bayes, E_PPGTnope gives EE its own NOPE, and RR keeps its fold-change reading. The companion vignette, Sampling depth, NOPE, and energy distance, runs a simulation study of each situation above.

Execution

Build a synthetic long counts table

We begin with a known enrichment structure. A synthetic long table carries one row per subject-category combination with columns subjectId, category, group, and n, matching the package’s default long-table schema. We draw subjects from a multinomial allocation within each group, so Control, Condition1, and Condition2 are approximately exchangeable before we impose any enrichment. We then multiply counts in Condition1 for Category0 by a fixed factor, introducing a modest, known enrichment in that group alone. We leave Condition2 unmodified, so its compositions remain exchangeable with Control under the generating process.

The internal functions build_synthetic_long_table() and plant_group_structure() live in the package namespace for vignette and test use; they are not exported, but they provide a reproducible procedure for simulating compositional cohorts.

library(HellingerDistanceEnrichment)

set.seed(26)
long_table <- HellingerDistanceEnrichment:::build_synthetic_long_table(
  n_subjects_per_group = 6,
  n_categories = 5,
  groups = c("Control", "Condition1", "Condition2"),
  seed = 26
)

long_table <- HellingerDistanceEnrichment:::plant_group_structure(
  long_table,
  target_group = "Condition1",
  target_category = "Category0",
  boost = 4
)

head(long_table)
#>     subjectId  category   group  n
#> 1 Control_S01 Category0 Control 12
#> 2 Control_S01 Category1 Control 20
#> 3 Control_S01 Category2 Control 27
#> 4 Control_S01 Category3 Control 23
#> 5 Control_S01 Category4 Control 18
#> 6 Control_S02 Category0 Control 18
table(unique(long_table[, c("subjectId", "group")])$group)
#> 
#> Condition1 Condition2    Control 
#>          6          6          6

The head of the table confirms the long format: each subject contributes KK rows (one per category), and the imposed enrichment appears as larger n in Condition1 for Category0 only. The subject-group table should show six subjects in each of the three groups.

Extract compositions and run permutation inference

ExtractClusterComposition() aggregates the long table to a CategoryComposition object, a subjects-by-categories count matrix with a named group factor. It records provenance and zero-fills missing subject-category combinations.

CompareGroupCompositions() accepts either a CategoryComposition or a long table directly. Here we extract first so you can inspect the subject-scale object before inference.

composition <- ExtractClusterComposition(long_table)
composition
#> CategoryComposition with 18 subjects, 5 categories, and 3 groups

perm_result <- CompareGroupCompositions(
  composition,
  method = "permutation",
  nPermutations = 500,
  seed = 42
)

perm_result
#> HellingerEnrichmentResult (permutation): omnibus effectSize=2.0873, pValue=0.0020
#>   omnibus energyDistance=0.0746 (squared Hellinger units)
#>   3 contrast(s) tested
perm_result$omnibus
#> $effectSize
#> [1] 2.087283
#> 
#> $energyDistance
#> [1] 0.07462467
#> 
#> $pValue
#> [1] 0.001996008
perm_result$contrasts
#>                 contrastId effectSize energyDistance      pValue       pAdj
#> 2 Condition1_vs_Condition2   2.652343   1.213565e-01 0.003992016 0.01197605
#> 3    Condition1_vs_Control   2.510626   1.024621e-01 0.003992016 0.01197605
#> 4    Condition2_vs_Control   1.002185   5.539422e-05 0.375249501 0.37524950

The printed HellingerEnrichmentResult summarizes the omnibus ratio and p-value. perm_result$omnibus holds the global effect size and unadjusted p-value; perm_result$contrasts holds all three pairwise contrasts with Holm-adjusted pAdj columns, listed in the order the package generates group-level pairs: Condition1_vs_Condition2, Condition1_vs_Control, Condition2_vs_Control. The imposed enrichment shows up at the omnibus level (effect size 2.09, p = 0.002) and in both Condition1 contrasts, for example Condition1_vs_Control (R = 2.51, pAdj = 0.012). Condition2_vs_Control, the arm we never modified, sits at R = 1.00 with pAdj = 0.38, consistent with exchangeability for a group whose composition we never altered.

Custom contrasts (and optional collapse)

Default output includes every pairwise contrast. Passing contrasts replaces that pairwise set with the comparisons you named; the omnibus test still runs. Holm adjustment on permutation pAdj then applies only to those rows. A length-2 character vector is enough for one pair (c("Control", "Condition1")). A named list helps when you want stable identifiers, or when a comparison is a collapse instead of a subset. With three groups, a natural planned family names the two primary comparisons: enriched versus Control, and the unmodified group versus Control.

perm_custom <- CompareGroupCompositions(
  composition,
  method = "permutation",
  nPermutations = 500,
  contrasts = list(
    condition1_vs_control = c("Control", "Condition1"),
    condition2_vs_control = c("Control", "Condition2")
  ),
  seed = 42
)

perm_custom$contrasts
#>              contrastId effectSize energyDistance      pValue        pAdj
#> 2 condition1_vs_control   2.510626   1.024621e-01 0.003992016 0.007984032
#> 3 condition2_vs_control   1.002185   5.539422e-05 0.385229541 0.385229541

perm_custom$contrasts contains those two rows instead of all three pairwises, so the unused Condition1_vs_Condition2 comparison does not consume a Holm penalty. Set includePairwise = TRUE if you need the old overlay (named specs plus every pairwise). Collapse becomes essential when you relabel experimental groups for analysis (for example, merging dose cohorts into a single treated group) without rebuilding the count matrix by hand; see ?CompareGroupCompositions for the collapse argument.

Bayesian approach

The Bayesian method reuses the same contrast specifications but replaces fixed compositions with Dirichlet posterior draws. For vignette execution time, keep nPosterior small; production analyses should raise it so posterior means and intervals stabilize.

bayes_result <- CompareGroupCompositions(
  composition,
  method = "bayes",
  nPosterior = 20,
  seed = 42
)

bayes_result$omnibus
#> $effectSize
#> [1] 1.63687
#> 
#> $PPGT1
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $R_PPGTnope
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $R_nopeHigh
#> [1] 1.132811
#> 
#> $R_hdiAboveNope

#> 
#> $E_PPGTnope
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $E_nopeHigh
#> [1] 0.02083857
#> 
#> $E_hdiAboveNope
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $enoughShufflesForNope
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $effectCiLow
#> [1] 1.485177
#> 
#> $effectCiHigh
#> [1] 1.768305
#> 
#> $energyDistance
#> [1] 0.07099183
#> 
#> $energyCiLow
#> [1] 0.05426503
#> 
#> $energyCiHigh
#> [1] 0.08177732
#> 
#> $draws
#>  [1] 1.708383 1.512447 1.629517 1.653181 1.612448 1.739634 1.768305 1.746784
#>  [9] 1.699903 1.667526 1.766796 1.554594 1.616840 1.567226 1.592179 1.485177
#> [17] 1.445179 1.719701 1.667845 1.583727
bayes_result$contrasts
#>                 contrastId effectSize PPGT1 R_PPGTnope R_nopeHigh
#> 2 Condition1_vs_Condition2  2.1807057  1.00       1.00   1.271343
#> 3    Condition1_vs_Control  2.0138347  1.00       1.00   1.250679
#> 4    Condition2_vs_Control  0.9866097  0.25       0.05   1.142103
#>   R_hdiAboveNope E_PPGTnope  E_nopeHigh E_hdiAboveNope enoughShufflesForNope
#> 2           TRUE       1.00 0.041741391           TRUE                  TRUE
#> 3           TRUE       1.00 0.036404736           TRUE                  TRUE
#> 4          FALSE       0.05 0.007847746          FALSE                  TRUE
#>   effectCiLow effectCiHigh energyDistance  energyCiLow energyCiHigh
#> 2   1.9125217     2.461328   0.1263427672  0.095355843   0.14684666
#> 3   1.7372538     2.263975   0.1075147607  0.081307826   0.13075750
#> 4   0.9101125     1.058920  -0.0009219148 -0.007514817   0.00312827

bayes_result$omnibus$effectSize is the posterior mean of RR over the Dirichlet draws; the permutation result reports RR at the softened point estimate. The interval effectCiLow to effectCiHigh is a 95% HPDI by default and shows whether R>1R > 1 holds up under composition uncertainty. When the interval excludes 1, PPGT1 is typically near 1; the interval width and bayes_result$omnibus$draws show whether that exclusion is a hair above 1 or a large enrichment. When the interval spans 1 but permutation p-values are small, sparse counts may be driving a fixed-composition signal that the Bayesian procedure weakens. R_PPGTnope sharpens the first case: it asks whether RR clears the edge that label shuffling routinely produces, so a posterior that sits a hair above 1 no longer reads as enrichment.

To set the edges yourself, pass a number above 1 as nope and a number above 0 as energyNope. Here ComputeEnergyNopeBound() translates a 5-point composition shift on five even categories into an EE bound:

reference_composition <- rep(0.2, 5)
shifted_composition <- c(0.15, 0.25, 0.2, 0.2, 0.2)
energy_edge <- ComputeEnergyNopeBound(reference_composition, shifted_composition)
energy_edge
#> [1] 0.006376243

fixed_nope_result <- CompareGroupCompositions(
  composition,
  method = "bayes",
  nPosterior = 20,
  nope = 1.2,
  energyNope = energy_edge,
  seed = 42
)
fixed_nope_result$contrasts[, c("contrastId", "PPGT1", "R_PPGTnope", "R_nopeHigh", "E_PPGTnope", "E_nopeHigh")]
#>                 contrastId PPGT1 R_PPGTnope R_nopeHigh E_PPGTnope  E_nopeHigh
#> 2 Condition1_vs_Condition2   1.0          1        1.2          1 0.006376243
#> 3    Condition1_vs_Control   1.0          1        1.2          1 0.006376243
#> 4    Condition2_vs_Control   0.3          0        1.2          0 0.006376243

Every contrast now shares the edges R=1.2R = 1.2 and EE = 0.0064. PPGT1 differs slightly from bayes_result despite the same seed, because only the NOPE run consumed extra random numbers for its shuffles. Translating a meaningful shift into a ratio needs a simulation at your own depths and group sizes, because RR also depends on within-group spread; the companion sampling-depth vignette shows how that spread moves RR.

Plot contrasts

PlotCompositionContrasts() stacks two panels that share the contrast rows: RR on top and EE below, each read left to right on its own axis. A dotted vertical line marks each statistic’s no-difference value, R=1R = 1 and E=0E = 0. When showOmnibus = TRUE (default), a dashed line in each panel marks the omnibus value; the RR panel labels it with the p-value (permutation) or PPGT1 and R_PPGTnope (Bayes), and the EE panel labels it with EE and, under Bayes, E_PPGTnope. Set showEnergyDistance = FALSE for the ratio panel alone.

PlotCompositionContrasts(perm_result)

Permutation contrasts on R (top) and E (bottom) with omnibus references.

For permutation results, the plot colors points by whether Holm-adjusted pAdj < 0.05. For Bayes results, half-eye plots show the posterior density of each contrast’s RR and EE with nested intervals, and a gray band behind each half-eye spans that statistic’s NOPE, permutation-calibrated or fixed: from 1 to R_nopeHigh in the top panel and from 0 to E_nopeHigh in the bottom panel. The legend names each band: “NOPE (permutation)” for the default, where the band shows the median of the per-draw edges, or “NOPE (fixed)”, in a darker gray, for a bound you supplied. The share of each slab right of its band approximates that statistic’s NOPE probability; it matches exactly for a fixed edge, while the NOPE compares each draw with its own edge.

PlotCompositionContrasts(bayes_result)

Bayesian half-eye posterior densities of R (top) and E (bottom), each with its NOPE band, for pairwise contrasts.

The two figures share the same scales, each with uncertainty suited to its method. Permutation marks discrete significance against the label null; Bayes shows composition uncertainty as half-eye densities of RR and EE. Reading the panels together separates the size of a shift (EE) from how far it stands out against within-group spread (RR).

Closing interpretation

On this synthetic cohort, both approaches recover the imposed Condition1 enrichment in Category0: the omnibus ratio and both Condition1 contrasts sit well above 1, with permutation p-values and Bayesian intervals agreeing that the shift is real. Condition2_vs_Control behaves as expected for a group that we never modified, and the two methods agree on it: permutation returns R = 1.00 with pAdj = 0.38, and the Bayesian interval spans 1 (0.91 to 1.06) with PPGT1 = 0.25, R_PPGTnope = 0.05, and E_PPGTnope = 0.05. A significant omnibus result therefore does not imply that every pairwise group differs from Control. The energy distance gives the same reading in absolute units: Condition1_vs_Control separates by E = 0.1 squared Hellinger units, while Condition2_vs_Control sits at E = 0.000055.

These results come from one synthetic cohort, and Bayes can sit on either side of permutation. Sparse categories, unequal cell yields, or violated exchangeability (for example, batch confounded with group) can produce ratios that look enriched under fixed compositions but fail to hold once we propagate Dirichlet uncertainty; there, Bayes can weaken a permutation signal. Dense counts with RR just above 1 produce the opposite disagreement: PPGT1 can sit near 1 while the HPDI barely excludes 1, and permutation still reports a large p-value because labels remain compatible with exchangeability. R_PPGTnope targets this case: it stays low when the excess over 1 is no larger than what label shuffling produces. Permutation also targets a fixed α\alpha: an exchangeable group will cross a p < 0.05 threshold by chance alone roughly one run in twenty, so an isolated marginal p-value from a single permutation run is weak evidence against exchangeability. The interval and the draws are how you judge closeness to 1; PPGT1 alone does not encode effect magnitude.

References

Kruschke, J. K. (2018). Rejecting or accepting parameter values in Bayesian estimation. Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(2), 270-280. https://doi.org/10.1177/2515245918771304. Article page (APS); open-access record (IU ScholarWorks).
